reason: The provided sources contain multiple cross-verified claims across different sites that support a narrative revealing how the famous myth of Mrs. O'Leary's cow was fabricated.
story: On October 8, 1871, a devastating blaze broke out on DeKoven Street in Chicago. Driven by severe drought and high winds, the Great Chicago Fire destroyed thousands of buildings, killed nearly 300 people, and left 100,000 homeless. Looking for a simple culprit, reporter Michael Ahern published a story claiming an Irish immigrant woman named Catherine O'Leary started the disaster when her cow kicked over a lantern in her barn. Rooted in widespread anti-Irish prejudice, the nation eagerly embraced the narrative. In reality, Catherine O'Leary was asleep in bed when the fire started, and the official investigation found no proof of her guilt. Decades later, Ahern publicly admitted he had fabricated the cow story for colorful news copy. Harassed and shamed, O'Leary spent her remaining years as a recluse until her death in 1895. It took until 1997 for the Chicago City Council to formally exonerate her.
angle: A reporter invented the famous story that Mrs. O'Leary's cow started the Great Chicago Fire, and even after he admitted making it up, Chicago took 126 years to formally exonerate her.

claims.claim: The Great Chicago Fire began on the evening of October 8, 1871, in a barn on DeKoven Street.
The property where the fire originated belonged to Irish immigrants Patrick and Catherine O'Leary.
Journalist Michael Ahern published the story claiming the fire was started when a cow kicked over a lantern.
Catherine O'Leary testified under oath that she was asleep in bed when the fire broke out.
Michael Ahern later admitted publicly that he had fabricated the cow and lantern story.
Anti-Irish sentiment in 1870s America contributed to Catherine O'Leary being singled out as a scapegoat.
The Great Chicago Fire killed approximately 300 people and left around 100,000 residents homeless.
Severe drought during the summer and autumn of 1871 made Chicago's predominantly wooden construction extremely flammable.
The official 1871 inquiry into the fire concluded that the exact cause could not be determined.
In 1997, 126 years after the fire, the Chicago City Council passed a resolution formally exonerating Catherine O'Leary.
Historians have proposed neighbor Daniel Peg Leg Sullivan as a possible alternative cause for starting the fire.
Due to persistent harassment and scapegoating, Catherine O'Leary lived as a recluse until her death in 1895.

disputed: The exact year and circumstances of reporter Michael Ahern's confession vary across sources (cited as 1893, 1911, or 1921, with some claiming it was ghostwritten) — script should attribute as 'according to later accounts' or leave out specific dates.

The true origin of the fire is unproven (theories include neighbor Daniel Peg Leg Sullivan, men gambling in the barn, or a meteor shower) — script should state that the official cause remains undetermined.
The name of O'Leary's cow (Daisy, Madeline, or Gwendolyn) is folklore — script should leave it out or label as legend.
